questions.stem: Heating an equilibrium mixture favours which direction?

options.text: The endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat
options.explanation: The system responds to heating by using up heat in the endothermic direction.

options.text: The exothermic direction, which releases more heat
options.explanation: Releasing heat would add to the disturbance, not oppose it.

options.text: Neither direction moves
options.explanation: Temperature shifts do move the balance.

options.text: Both directions equally
options.explanation: Equal shifts would change nothing, which is not observed.

questions.stem: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. What does cooling the mixture do?

options.text: It favours the forward reaction, so more product forms
options.explanation: Cooling favours the heat-releasing side, which is the forward direction here.

options.text: It favours the backward reaction, so more reactant forms
options.explanation: The backward reaction is endothermic here and is favoured by heating.

options.text: The mixture changes colour to blue
options.explanation: Colour depends on the specific equilibrium, not on cooling alone.

options.text: The equilibrium is destroyed
options.explanation: The balance moves; it does not vanish.

questions.stem: What does it mean for the position of equilibrium to shift right?

options.text: The forward reaction is favoured, so the amount of products increases
options.explanation: Right shifts enrich the product side of the equation.

options.text: The reactants increase in amount
options.explanation: That describes a left shift.

options.text: The reaction stops completely
options.explanation: Equilibrium mixtures never stop reacting.

options.text: The catalyst becomes more active
options.explanation: Catalysts do not take sides in the shift.

questions.stem: Iodine monochloride and chlorine form iodine trichloride, with the forward reaction exothermic. On heating, the brown colour deepens. Why?

options.text: Heating favours the endothermic backward reaction, so more brown reactant forms
options.explanation: The shift runs left, enriching the dark brown starting materials.

options.text: Heating favours the forward reaction, so more yellow product forms
options.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic and is disfavoured by heating.

options.text: The product decomposes into oxygen
options.explanation: No oxygen is part of this equilibrium.

options.text: The thermometer itself darkens the liquid
options.explanation: The colour change is chemical, not instrumental.

questions.stem: Which change would shift an equilibrium towards the exothermic direction?

options.text: Lowering the temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Cooling pulls the balance towards the heat-releasing side.

options.text: Raising the temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic side instead.

options.text: Adding a catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts never move the position.

options.text: Increasing the pressure of a gas equilibrium
options.explanation: Pressure shifts follow molecule counts, not heat.

questions.stem: Why does increased pressure favour fewer gas molecules?

options.text: Fewer molecules ease the crowding that the pressure increase created
options.explanation: The shift opposes the squeeze by reducing the gas count.

options.text: Fewer molecules are always faster
options.explanation: Speed is not the logic; the count is.

options.text: Because solids take up the extra pressure
options.explanation: Solids and liquids are unaffected by pressure changes here.

options.text: Because molecules shrink under pressure
options.explanation: Molecules do not shrink; the balance moves.

questions.stem: In 2NO2 (g) turning into N2O4 (g), what does increased pressure do?

options.text: It favours the forward reaction, since two molecules become one
options.explanation: The product side holds fewer gas molecules, so pressure pushes the balance right.

options.text: It favours the backward reaction, since one molecule becomes two
options.explanation: Splitting into more molecules works against a squeeze.

options.text: Nothing, because both sides have equal counts
options.explanation: The counts are 2 and 1, not equal.

options.text: It turns the gas into a liquid
options.explanation: The equilibrium stays gaseous.

questions.stem: A gaseous equilibrium has three molecules on the left and three on the right. What does increased pressure do?

options.text: Nothing to the position, because both sides hold the same gas count
options.explanation: Equal counts leave the balance unmoved by pressure.

options.text: It shifts the position to the left
options.explanation: No side has fewer molecules to favour.

options.text: It shifts the position to the right
options.explanation: The equal count blocks any shift.

options.text: It stops the forward reaction
options.explanation: Reactions continue at equilibrium regardless.

questions.stem: Which observation would show a gaseous equilibrium shifting right after compression?

options.text: The colour deepens towards the product side of the equation
options.explanation: Enrichment of the product side shows itself as that side's colour strengthening.

options.text: The colour lightens towards the reactant side
options.explanation: That would indicate a left shift.

options.text: The gas turns into a solid
options.explanation: State changes are not part of the shift.

options.text: The readings become impossible to take
options.explanation: Compression leaves the mixture observable.

questions.stem: Pressure changes do not affect the position when which condition holds?

options.text: The same number of moles of gas sits on each side of the equation
options.explanation: Matching gas counts leave the balance with nothing to prefer.

options.text: A catalyst is present in the mixture
options.explanation: Catalysts are irrelevant to pressure shifts.

options.text: The temperature is above room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature level does not cancel pressure effects.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic
options.explanation: Heat direction governs temperature shifts, not pressure ones.

questions.stem: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of equilibrium?

options.text: None: the position is unchanged
options.explanation: Catalysts speed arrival at equilibrium without moving it.

options.text: It shifts the position to the right
options.explanation: That would require favouring the forward direction, which catalysts never do.

options.text: It shifts the position to the left
options.explanation: No direction is favoured.

options.text: It depends on which catalyst is used
options.explanation: Every catalyst behaves the same way here.

questions.stem: Why does a catalyst fail to move the equilibrium position?

options.text: It increases the rate of both the forward and backward reactions by the same amount
options.explanation: Equal speeding leaves the balance between the two untouched.

options.text: It is too small an amount to matter
options.explanation: Amount is irrelevant to the symmetry of the effect.

options.text: It stops both reactions completely
options.explanation: Catalysts speed reactions, never stop them.

options.text: It only helps the reverse reaction
options.explanation: Help is shared equally between directions.

questions.stem: What does a catalyst change about an equilibrium system?

options.text: The time taken to reach equilibrium
options.explanation: Faster arrival is the one change a catalyst delivers.

options.text: The final amount of product at equilibrium
options.explanation: The equilibrium composition is identical either way.

options.text: The enthalpy change of the forward reaction
options.explanation: Energy differences between levels are untouched.

options.text: The colour of the final mixture
options.explanation: The same final composition has the same colour.

questions.stem: On a graph of product amount against time, how does the catalysed run compare with the uncatalysed one?

options.text: It flattens sooner but reaches the identical final level
options.explanation: Faster approach with the same destination is the catalytic fingerprint.

options.text: It flattens later at a higher level
options.explanation: Neither the timing nor the level changes that way.

options.text: It never flattens
options.explanation: Equilibrium is still reached, only sooner.

options.text: It starts from a higher point
options.explanation: Both runs begin with no product.

questions.stem: Why is the equilibrium composition the same with and without a catalyst?

options.text: The same balance between forward and backward rates is restored once equilibrium returns
options.explanation: Equilibrium composition depends on conditions, not on how quickly they are met.

options.text: Because catalysts remove the reverse reaction
options.explanation: Both directions continue at equilibrium.

options.text: Because catalysts change the temperature
options.explanation: Catalysts are not heat sources.

options.text: Because products destroy the catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts survive the reaction unchanged.
